The blade comes free with a rasp that cuts the wind, and then you are running.

Ash sprays under your boots. The trail drops and the wreck rises to meet you, a lead wagon slewed sideways with its axle snapped, canvas slashed open and spilling bolts of dyed cloth into the muck. A driver hangs dead over the footboard with his throat opened. Two others kneel in the ruts, wrists already looped in cord, and a slaver stands over them working the collar-hook like a man tying a bundle of firewood.

He hears you. He turns. He is broad and scarred and he wears a leather harness studded with old iron rings, and the grin that splits his beard is the grin of a man who has just found money in the road.

[SAY:Kadrun Zethran]"By every hell," he says, and he does not even lift his weapon. "Korrag. The Northlander. Still walking about loose."

The name goes into you like a splinter. You know that voice. You heard it through the bars of a holding pen for three winters, calling out the odds on whether you would live the night.

His men fan out from the wagons, four of them, blades low and eyes on their master. Kadrun Zethran spreads his empty hands wide, delighted.

[SAY:Kadrun Zethran]"Put the steel down and hear me. Valerius pays better now than he ever did. Come back and be a wolf again, Northlander. You were never one of the sheep."

You are already running and you do not stop.

Kadrun's grin holds a heartbeat too long. He expected the pause, the word, the flicker of a man weighing coin against conscience. He gets four feet of Northlander steel instead.

[SAY:Korrag]"I heard you," you say. "Answer's no."

The nearest slaver steps into your path with his blade coming up crosswise. You do not slow. Your shoulder takes him in the chest and the ash goes out from under his heels, and your longsword opens him from hip to ribs on the way past. He folds around the wound and the wind takes his cry apart.

The other three come alive at once, spreading wide to flank, boots churning gray. Behind them Kadrun draws a heavy notched falchion and laughs, and the sound is worse than the screaming horse.

[SAY:Kadrun Zethran]"Alive, you dogs! The Master wants him breathing!"

You give him no chance to be clever. Your weight drops, your grip shortens, and you bring the longsword over in a stroke that starts at your heels and ends somewhere past his shoulder. Bone parts. The blade goes through his collarbone and buries itself in his chest, and the shock of it runs up your arms like a hammer striking an anvil. He is dead before the ash settles around his knees.

You wrench the steel free with a foot on his ribs. Two slavers left standing, and neither wants to be the next one forward. They circle instead, spreading wide, and one whistles sharp through his teeth toward the wagons.

Kadrun does not circle. He walks in through the gray drift with the falchion resting on his shoulder, unhurried, still smiling under the beard.

You give ground for the first time, and you give it fast.

Three long strides back and the broken lead wagon takes your shoulders, splintered oak and slashed canvas at your spine. Now nothing comes at you from behind. The flanking dies right there, and you see the understanding go through the two slavers like cold water. They wanted your back. They will have to come and buy it.

One tries. He lunges along the wagon's wheel with a short blade darting for your thigh, low, aiming to cripple and not kill. You catch his wrist on your crossguard and drive your elbow into his face. Cartilage crunches. He reels away into the ruts spitting teeth and blood, and his fellow drags him back by the harness before you can finish it.

Kadrun halts ten feet out. He looks at the wagon, at your braced stance, and something ugly and appreciative moves behind his eyes.

[SAY:Kadrun Zethran]"There it is." He spits into the ash. "That's the beast that made me money."

Behind him, one of the kneeling captives has worked her wrists half loose, and she is watching you with the flat stillness of someone waiting for one chance only.

You set your boot against the snapped axle and let the wreck do the work of three men.

The wagon bed cants over your left side. The broken shaft juts from the ruts at your right like a spear driven into the earth. Between them there is a gap wide enough for one man, and one man only, and you fill it with steel and shoulders and nothing else. The wind screams down the trail and drags ash across your eyes and you do not blink.

The bloodied one comes because his master is watching and fear of Kadrun is heavier than fear of you. He crowds into the gap. There is no room for his blade to swing and no room for him to turn, and you put the longsword through his belly and lift, and his boots leave the ground. He hangs there a moment making a sound with no words in it. Then you shake him off the blade and he sprawls across the axle and stops moving.

The last of the pack does not come. He backs away with his eyes gone white at the edges, and then he turns and runs east into the ash-drift, and Kadrun lets him go without a glance.

[SAY:Kadrun Zethran]"Cheap men. Cheap as they come." He rolls the falchion off his shoulder into a two-handed grip, and now he is not smiling at all. "Fine. Alive is a preference, not an order."

At the far wagon the bound woman gets one hand free. She reaches, slow and careful, for a dead slaver's knife lying six inches from her knee.

You do not move out of the gap. You spit ash off your lip and let him hear you.

[SAY:Korrag]"Made you money." Your voice comes flat as a butcher's block. "You never bled once. You stood at the rail and shouted numbers while other men opened each other. Twelve fights. Every one of them mine. Every coin yours."

The wind takes the ash between you and drags it sideways.

[SAY:Korrag]"You did not make a copper, Kadrun. You collected it. There is a difference, and it is standing in front of you with a sword."

Something goes out of his face. Not fear, he has too little imagination for fear, but the easy contempt drops off it like a mask coming loose, and what is underneath is small and hot and old. Sixteen feet of ruts and dead men lie between you, and he comes across them faster than a man his size has any right to move.

The falchion arrives in a flat sweeping arc aimed at your ribs, and it is not the stroke of a rail-shouter. It is a killing cut, practiced ten thousand times. You take it on the crossguard high and the shock jolts down into your boots. Steel screams on steel. He drives his shoulder in after it and the wagon groans at your back.

Behind him the woman's fingers close on the knife hilt.

[SAY:Kadrun Zethran]"Twelve fights," he snarls into your face. "And I remember every one, because I watched you learn to enjoy it."

You hold the falchion locked on your crossguard and turn your head six inches, no more.

[SAY:Korrag]"Woman! The cord, not the man! Cut yourself loose and run west!"

Kadrun's eyes flick. It is a small thing, a half-heartbeat of attention thrown backward over his shoulder, but a man committed to a shoulder-drive cannot afford half a heartbeat. You surge up out of the brace and throw him off you. He staggers two steps into the ruts and has to plant his boot on a corpse to keep his feet.

Behind him the knife saws through hemp. The woman comes up off her knees fast and low, but she does not run west. She grabs the second captive by the collar and hauls him upright, and the two of them stumble toward the far wagon with the knife still red in her fist.

You do not meet him. You slide backward along the wagon bed, sword low, drawing him after you.

Kadrun follows because rage will not let him do anything else. He comes through the gap you spent three men to hold, and the broken axle waits for him there under six inches of drifted ash. His boot catches the shaft. His weight is already forward and there is nowhere for it to go but down, and he pitches into the ruts on one knee with the falchion flung wide for balance.

You are on him before the ash settles.

The longsword comes down in a two-handed chop that would split a shield rim. He gets the falchion up crossways and the blades ring like a hammer on a forge, and the force of it drives him flat onto his back in the mud. You feel the shock all the way to your teeth.
